drills.q: Recite the five buckets of the 50-question HR canon in order, with question ranges.
drills.a: Introduction & background (1-10), Career goals & motivation (11-20), Work experience & behavior (21-30), Teamwork & communication (31-40), Salary/availability/closing (41-50).

drills.q: Give your 'tell me about yourself' in the 90-second three-beat shape.
drills.a: Now (one sentence with scale) -> one proof-point project -> why this role. Ends handing the floor back. Not a chronological autobiography.

drills.q: A candidate says 'I'm leaving because my manager was toxic and there were no hikes.' What's wrong and what's the replacement sentence?
drills.a: Backward-push blame -- the only unrecoverable flag, true or not. Replace with forward-pull: 'I've taken the platform as far as the role allows; this role owns the serving layer I built toward.'

drills.q: The recruiter asks for salary expectations first. Walk through the deflection-and-anchor sequence.
drills.a: Deflect once ('I'd like to understand the band for the level'), then anchor from research: current fixed + target market range for the level (from levels/contacts BEFORE the call). Never a bare unanchored number -- the first number spoken is the one typed.

drills.q: What are the two questions you carry into 'do you have any questions for us?', and why those two?
drills.a: 'What does the first 90 days look like?' and 'What's the biggest gap between the job ad and the day-to-day?' Neither is answerable by the website; both signal seriousness. 'No questions' is scored as low interest.

drills.q: The interviewer asks 'why are you leaving?' twice, ten minutes apart. What is the second ask actually testing?
drills.a: Consistency: the re-ask catches embellishment. Two different stories = dishonesty flag worse than either story. Same sentence, verbatim, both times.

drills.q: A candidate answers the weakness question with 'I'm a perfectionist.' Why does this fail, and what replaces it?
drills.a: Fake weakness = evading the question while announcing you prepare. Replace: one real, non-fatal, work-in-progress weakness + mitigation in present tense ('I under-document early prototypes; I now write the README before the second user asks').

drills.q: Why does 'have you ever missed a deadline?' test communication rather than failure, and what does the passing answer contain?
drills.a: The silent missed deadline is the firing offense; the well-communicated one is an incident. Pass: yes-once + cause + who was told and WHEN (before it passed) + what changed after. 'Never missed one' reads as unreflective.

drills.q: The interviewer asks 'why should we choose you over other candidates?' and the candidate criticizes the hypothetical others. What flag fires?
drills.a: The same bitterness flag as the leaving-reason -- criticism of others (even hypothetical) reads as grievance. Correct: Q3's fit case compressed to one sentence + one pool-differentiator, never the competition.

drills.q: Explain why an HR screen is a checklist, not a rubric, and name the one preparation consequence.
drills.a: The interviewer fills form blanks (logistics, flags, salary box) -- no drilling, no partial credit for method. Consequence: every question is predictable in advance, so failing one is a preparation failure scored identically to a competence failure.

drills.q: Walk the disagreement-with-manager ladder, including the trap after the call goes against you and fails as you predicted.
drills.a: State the case with evidence once; if overruled, record dissent in the decision doc; commit fully. When it fails: help fix it with zero reference to the prediction -- 'I told you so' converts a good process answer into a personality flag.

drills.q: Why do teamwork questions (31-40) get asked as a group, and what does a pushover-Q34 + warrior-Q35 pattern signal?
drills.a: They're cross-checked for one consistent personality. The contradiction reads as scripted answers per question rather than one person describing real behavior -- consistency across the bucket is the actual test.
